AAL Sales Analysis: Q4 2020 (Australia)¶

Business context. AAL (Australian Apparel, est. 2000) is planning to expand. The CEO asked the head of Sales & Marketing to:

  1. Identify the states that bring in the most revenue.
  2. Design sales programs for the states that bring in the least.

Data. AusApparalSales4thQrt2020.csv has transactions from 1 Oct to 30 Dec 2020, broken down by State, customer Group (Kids, Men, Women, Seniors) and Time of day (Morning, Afternoon, Evening).

Workflow. 1) Data wrangling, 2) Data analysis, 3) Data visualization (dashboard), 4) Recommendations.

Findings.

  • No values are missing: isna() is 0 and notna() is 7,560 in every column.
  • The text columns have a leading space (" WA", " Kids"), which would break filters and joins. We strip it.
  • Date is stored as a string. We convert it to datetime so we can resample by week and month.
  • Every row has a fixed price of AUD 2,500 per unit. So Sales = 2,500 × Unit, which means the two columns tell the same story.
  • No negative or zero values, no duplicate rows.
In [6]:
for c in ["Time", "State", "Group"]:
    df[c] = df[c].str.strip()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%d-%b-%Y")
df["Time"] = pd.Categorical(df["Time"], ["Morning", "Afternoon", "Evening"], ordered=True)
df["Month"] = df["Date"].dt.month_name()
df["Week"] = df["Date"].dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int)

1b. How to treat missing or incorrect data¶

This dataset has none, but if it did:

  • Missing Sales with Unit present (or the other way round): fill it from the fixed 2,500 price. The value can be recovered exactly.
  • Missing numbers otherwise: fill with the median for that State × Group × Time. The median holds up better than the mean against the right-skewed sales distribution.
  • Missing State, Group, Date: drop the row. The record can't be placed in any analysis cell, and guessing a category would bias the state comparisons.
  • Incorrect values (negative units, typo categories): fix them where the right value is clear (e.g. map "wa" to "WA"), otherwise drop and log them.
  • Drop rows only when they're a small share (< ~5%). Otherwise fill, so we don't change the shape of the data.

1c. Normalization¶

We use Min-Max normalization, which rescales a column to [0, 1]: $x' = \frac{x - x_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}}$.

It keeps the shape of the distribution and puts Unit and Sales on the same scale. That makes them comparable and ready for distance-based models, such as clustering states for sales programs. Standardization (z-score) assumes roughly normal data, and this data is skewed, so normalization suits it better.

In [7]:
num = ["Unit", "Sales"]
norm = (df[num] - df[num].min()) / (df[num].max() - df[num].min())
df[["Unit_norm", "Sales_norm"]] = norm
df[["Unit", "Sales", "Unit_norm", "Sales_norm"]].describe()

1d. GroupBy for chunking vs merging¶

  • Chunking (split, apply, combine): groupby() splits the 7,560 rows into pieces (per state, group, time slot), runs an aggregation on each, and combines the results. That's the main tool for this problem: every business question here ("which state", "which group", "which time slot") is a group-wise aggregate.
  • Merging: groupby().transform() sends a group statistic back to each row, for example each row's share of its state total, with no explicit merge. It's also how we'd build summary tables to merge with outside data like state population or store counts.

Recommendation: use groupby for chunking and aggregation as the main technique, and use transform/merge only when you need row-level context (shares, benchmarks).

In [8]:
# Chunking: aggregate per state
state_sum = df.groupby("State")["Sales"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"]).sort_values("sum", ascending=False)
# Merging back: each row's share of its state's revenue
df["State_share_%"] = df["Sales"] / df.groupby("State")["Sales"].transform("sum") * 100
state_sum

Is the gap between states statistically real? One-way ANOVA on transaction-level sales:

In [13]:
f, p = stats.f_oneway(*[g["Sales"].values for _, g in df.groupby("State")])
f2, p2 = stats.f_oneway(*[g["Sales"].values for _, g in df.groupby("Group")])
print(f"State: F={f:,.1f}, p={p:.2e}  ->  {'significant' if p < .05 else 'not significant'}")
print(f"Group: F={f2:,.2f}, p={p2:.3f}  ->  {'significant' if p2 < .05 else 'not significant'}")

State: F=3,662.6, p=0.00e+00  ->  significant
Group: F=0.28, p=0.838  ->  not significant

3. Data visualization: S&M dashboard¶

Why Seaborn. It's built on Matplotlib and takes pandas DataFrames directly, so grouped and statistical plots (box plots, distributions, heatmaps, confidence intervals) take one line each and come with consistent, readable styling. That fits a statistical analysis like this one. It also renders inside JupyterLab with no extra setup. Plotly would add interactivity but is heavier and less suited to static statistical reports. Matplotlib is used underneath for the subplot layout.

3.1 State-wise sales by demographic group¶

4. Insights and recommendations¶

In [23]:
lo = st[st < st.mean()].index.tolist()
hi = st[st >= st.mean()].index.tolist()
print("Above-average states:", hi)
print("Below-average states:", lo)
print(f"Top 2 states share of revenue: {st.iloc[:2].sum()/st.sum()*100:.1f}%")

Above-average states: ['VIC', 'NSW', 'SA']
Below-average states: ['QLD', 'TAS', 'NT', 'WA']
Top 2 states share of revenue: 53.1%

Key findings

  1. Revenue is concentrated. VIC leads with 31% of Q4 revenue and NSW follows with 22%, so the top two bring in about 53%. SA (17%) is the only other state above the state average. QLD (10%) is mid-tier. TAS, NT and WA each bring in about 6.5%, and VIC sells about 4.8× what WA does. The ANOVA confirms the state gap is significant (p < 0.001).
  2. Groups are balanced. Men, Women, Kids and Seniors each contribute about 25%. The spread from highest (Men) to lowest (Seniors) is only 2%, and the ANOVA shows no significant difference (p = 0.84). The product mix is fine. Geography is what's driving revenue.
  3. Time of day is almost flat. Morning (33.6%) is the narrow peak, Afternoon is close behind, and Evening (32.9%) is off-peak. The same pattern holds in every state. Evening is the one slot with clear room to grow.
  4. Seasonality. November fell 21% from October, then December rose 49% (holiday season). The four weeks to 27 Dec are the strongest of the quarter. The first and last weeks in the weekly table are partial weeks, so they look low.

Recommendations for the S&M head

  • Expansion: focus new-store and inventory investment on VIC and NSW, where demand is proven. Use SA, then QLD, as the next tier for growth.
  • Programs for low-revenue states (QLD, TAS, NT, WA):
    • Run the December-style holiday campaign earlier (late Oct to Nov) to fill the November dip, which hits these states hardest (down about 30–36% from October).
    • Offer evening-hour promotions (after-work events, extended-hours discounts) to lift the off-peak slot.
    • Use hyper-personalised / Next Best Offer campaigns through the loyalty CRM. With groups balanced, target households (family bundles across Kids, Women, Men, Seniors) rather than single segments.
    • Before adding stores, check whether the gap comes from population or from under-penetration. Merge state-level population and store counts into the groupby summary to get sales per capita and per store.
  • Staffing: put peak staff on Morning and Afternoon shifts, and use Evenings for promotional events.
  • Next steps: compare against Q4 2019 to separate growth from seasonality, and add store and product-category detail when it's available.
